subject: geography

moments.title: World Commission on Environment and Development
moments.who: Gro Harlem Brundtland, then Prime Minister of Norway
moments.body: UN Secretary-General Pérez de Cuéllar asks Brundtland to chair a commission to bridge the gap between environmental concerns of the North and developmental concerns of the South.
moments.takeaway: Until the 1980s, environment and development had often been treated as opposed. The Brundtland Commission tried to reframe them as inseparable.

moments.title: Our Common Future
moments.body: The report 'Our Common Future' is published in April 1987. It coins the most widely used definition of sustainable development.

quote.text: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

moments.takeaway: The definition is deliberately broad — useful as a framing principle, contested in implementation. Critics argue it allows greenwashing of conventional growth.

now.title: A keyword in policy
now.body: 'Sustainable development' is now in every major international agreement: the Rio Earth Summit (1992), the MDGs (2000), the Paris Agreement (2015), the Sustainable Development Goals (2015). The 'three pillars' framing — economic, social, environmental — comes out of the Brundtland legacy.
now.open_questions: Is the definition strong enough? 'Strong sustainability' theorists (Herman Daly) argue natural capital cannot be substituted by human capital and that current practice ignores this. 'Weak sustainability' approaches dominate policy.

reflection: Definitions can shape entire policy fields. The Brundtland sentence is recited in textbooks, statutes and corporate reports worldwide. Its slipperiness is part of its political success — and part of its limit.
